questions.title: Why neostigmine reverses competitive neuromuscular blockers
questions.question: Which of the following explains the wide use of neostigmine in reversing the action of competitive neuromuscular blockers used in surgical operations?

options.A: A better return of memory after operation
options.C: Its good CNS penetration leading to better recovery
options.D: Anti-muscarinic actions leading to decreased secretions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neostigmine is a quaternary compound that does not enter the CNS, so it has no effect on postoperative memory.
explanations.B: Correct. Competitive (non-depolarising) blockers such as vecuronium work by antagonising acetylcholine at the nicotinic end-plate. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising the concentration of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction so that it out-competes the blocker and restores transmission. This anticholinesterase action is exactly why it reverses the block.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neostigmine's lack of CNS penetration is a feature, but it is not the mechanism of reversal, which occurs peripherally at the junction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antimuscarinic action is not a property of neostigmine; atropine or glycopyrrolate is added separately to cover its muscarinic effects.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that neostigmine reverses non-depolarising blockade by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and raising junctional acetylcholine.

questions.title: Receptor whose stimulation lowers intracellular cAMP
questions.question: A decrease in intracellular cAMP results from stimulation of which of the following receptors?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Beta2 receptors couple to Gs and INCREASE cAMP via adenylyl cyclase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha1 receptors couple to Gq and act through phospholipase C (IP3/DAG and calcium), not by lowering cAMP.
explanations.C: Correct. M2 muscarinic receptors couple to the inhibitory Gi protein, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and so DECREASES intracellular cAMP; they also open potassium channels. This is the basis of the vagal slowing of the heart. Among the options only M2 stimulation lowers cAMP.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nn (neuronal nicotinic) receptors are ligand-gated ion channels; they depolarise the cell rather than acting through cAMP.

questions.learning_objective: Identify M2 muscarinic receptors as Gi-coupled receptors that decrease intracellular cAMP.

questions.title: Therapeutic use of pilocarpine (sialagogue)
questions.question: Which of the following describes a therapeutic use of the cholinomimetic alkaloid pilocarpine?

options.B: A mydriatic in cases of glaucoma
options.D: As an add-on therapy for cases of Parkinsonism

explanations.A: Correct. Pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic agonist that stimulates exocrine (salivary) glands, so it is used as a sialagogue to relieve xerostomia (dry mouth), for example after head-and-neck irradiation or in Sjogren syndrome. This glandular-secretory action is a recognised therapeutic use. It also lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma by causing MIOSIS, not mydriasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pilocarpine is a MIOTIC (pupil-constricting) agent in glaucoma, not a mydriatic; the term in this option is wrong.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pilocarpine does not inhibit hair growth; that is eflornithine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Parkinsonism is treated by reducing cholinergic tone with antimuscarinics, so a muscarinic agonist would worsen it.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise pilocarpine's use as a sialagogue for dry mouth and that it is a miotic, not a mydriatic.

questions.title: Why pralidoxime works in organophosphate poisoning
questions.question: Which of the following explains the use of pralidoxime in the treatment of organophosphorus poisoning?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pralidoxime is not a sedative; sedation in organophosphate poisoning is provided by a benzodiazepine such as diazepam.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The antimuscarinic component of therapy is atropine; pralidoxime has no antimuscarinic action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anticonvulsant cover is again the role of diazepam, not pralidoxime.
explanations.D: Correct. Organophosphates phosphorylate and inactivate acetylcholinesterase. Pralidoxime is an oxime that binds the phosphorylated enzyme and removes the phosphate group, REACTIVATING cholinesterase before irreversible 'ageing' occurs. This restores acetylcholine breakdown and relieves especially the nicotinic (muscle) features that atropine cannot touch, which is why it is given early.

questions.learning_objective: State that pralidoxime treats organophosphate poisoning by reactivating cholinesterase before ageing.

questions.title: Contraindication of atropine
questions.question: Contraindications of atropine include which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine is used to TREAT symptomatic bradycardia and some heart block, so this is an indication, not a contraindication.
explanations.B: Correct. Atropine relaxes the ciliary muscle and dilates the pupil, which crowds the iridocorneal angle and impairs aqueous drainage, raising intraocular pressure. In angle-closure glaucoma this can precipitate an acute dangerous rise in pressure, so glaucoma is a classic contraindication to atropine. This is why antimuscarinics are avoided or used with great caution in such patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Organophosphate poisoning is a principal INDICATION for atropine, not a contraindication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics reduce gut motility and can be used symptomatically in some diarrhoeas, so diarrhoea is not a contraindication.

questions.learning_objective: Identify glaucoma as a contraindication to atropine because of raised intraocular pressure.

questions.title: Ocular effect of antimuscarinic eye drops
questions.question: Which of the following is expected when using parasympathetic depressants as eye drops?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics block the sphincter pupillae and cause mydriasis (dilatation), not constriction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By crowding the drainage angle they tend to RAISE intraocular pressure, not lower it.
explanations.C: Correct. Antimuscarinic (parasympathetic-depressant) eye drops paralyse the ciliary muscle, producing cycloplegia so the lens cannot accommodate for near vision. Loss of accommodation, together with mydriasis, is the expected ocular effect and is exploited for refraction and fundus examination. It is the correct answer here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics cause bronchodilation, not bronchospasm, and topical eye drops have little systemic airway effect anyway.

questions.learning_objective: State that antimuscarinic eye drops cause cycloplegia (loss of accommodation) and mydriasis.

questions.title: How hyoscine differs from atropine on the CNS
questions.question: Compared to atropine, hyoscine is more likely to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyoscine is used to PREVENT nausea and vomiting (motion sickness), not to induce it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atropine has the stronger cardiac vagolytic effect and is more likely to cause tachycardia; hyoscine affects the heart less.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Central excitation and convulsions at toxic doses are more characteristic of atropine; hyoscine is depressant at therapeutic doses.
explanations.D: Correct. Hyoscine (scopolamine) penetrates the CNS well and at therapeutic doses causes sedation, drowsiness and amnesia, a central DEPRESSANT effect. Atropine, by contrast, tends to be centrally stimulant. This difference is why hyoscine is chosen as a sedative antiemetic and premedicant.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast hyoscine's central depressant effect with atropine's central stimulation.

questions.title: Anticholinesterase used in Alzheimer's disease
questions.question: Which of the following is an anticholinesterase used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyridostigmine is a peripherally acting quaternary anticholinesterase used in myasthenia gravis; it does not cross into the CNS to help dementia.
explanations.B: Correct. Rivastigmine is a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase (and butyrylcholinesterase) inhibitor that raises acetylcholine in the brain and is licensed for Alzheimer's disease, along with donepezil and galantamine. Its CNS penetration is what makes it useful for cognition. It is the correct choice here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tropicamide is a short-acting antimuscarinic mydriatic, not an anticholinesterase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Echothiophate is an irreversible organophosphate anticholinesterase used topically in glaucoma, not for dementia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify rivastigmine as a centrally acting anticholinesterase used in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.title: Antimuscarinic precipitating retention in prostatic hypertrophy
questions.question: An elderly man with benign prostatic hypertrophy recently complained of recurrent intestinal colic. A drug was prescribed but caused acute urine retention. Which of the following could be the prescribed drug?

explanations.A: Correct. Intestinal colic is treated with an antispasmodic antimuscarinic such as atropine, which relaxes gut smooth muscle. However, by also relaxing the bladder detrusor and reducing voiding, an antimuscarinic can precipitate acute retention in a man whose outflow is already narrowed by prostatic hypertrophy. This links the colic treatment to the retention, making atropine the offending drug.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neostigmine increases cholinergic tone and promotes bladder emptying; it would relieve, not cause, retention.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Propranolol is a beta-blocker used for cardiovascular indications; it is not an antispasmodic for colic and does not typically cause acute retention.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carbachol is a cholinergic agonist that stimulates the detrusor and promotes voiding, the opposite of causing retention.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that antimuscarinics can precipitate acute urinary retention in benign prostatic hypertrophy.

questions.title: Expected effects of atropine in organophosphate poisoning
questions.question: In a patient with organophosphorus poisoning, which of the following pharmacological effects would you expect after treatment with atropine?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atropine blocks vagal muscarinic tone at the heart, so it produces tachycardia, not bradycardia, though the bronchodilatation is correct.
explanations.B: Correct. Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, so in organophosphate poisoning it reverses the excess muscarinic stimulation: blocking cardiac M2 receptors raises heart rate (tachycardia) and blocking airway M3 receptors relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and dries secretions (bronchodilatation). This pairing of tachycardia and bronchodilatation is the expected antimuscarinic response.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypotension and bronchoconstriction are features of the cholinergic crisis itself, which atropine reverses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bradycardia and hypotension are the untreated muscarinic effects, the opposite of what atropine produces.

questions.learning_objective: Predict tachycardia and bronchodilatation as the antimuscarinic effects of atropine in organophosphate poisoning.
